title: Design SQL
description:
# Design SQL

You are given `n` tables represented by two arrays `names` and `columns`. `names[i]` is the name of the `i-th` table, and `columns[i]` is the number of columns in that table.

Implement the `SQL` class. Each table stores rows with an auto-incrementing `rowId`. Row ids are independent per table, start at `1`, and are never reused, even if an earlier row is deleted.

The class must support these operations:

* `SQL(List<String> names, List<Integer> columns)` initializes the tables.
* `void insertRow(String name, List<String> row)` inserts `row` into table `name` using the next row id for that table.
* `void deleteRow(String name, int rowId)` deletes the row with id `rowId` from table `name`.
* `String selectCell(String name, int rowId, int columnId)` returns the value in row `rowId` and column `columnId` from table `name`.

`columnId` is 1-indexed. It is guaranteed that every operation names an existing table. Every inserted row has exactly the table's column count. `deleteRow` is called only for an existing row, and `selectCell` is called only for an existing row and valid column.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["SQL", "insertRow", "selectCell", "insertRow", "deleteRow", "selectCell"]
[[["one", "two", "three"], [2, 3, 1]], ["two", ["first", "second", "third"]], ["two", 1, 3], ["two", ["fourth", "fifth", "sixth"]], ["two", 1], ["two", 2, 2]]

**Output:**
[null, null, "third", null, null, "fifth"]

**Explanation:**
SQL sql = new SQL(["one", "two", "three"], [2, 3, 1]);
sql.insertRow("two", ["first", "second", "third"]); // rowId 1 in table "two"
sql.selectCell("two", 1, 3); // returns "third"
sql.insertRow("two", ["fourth", "fifth", "sixth"]); // rowId 2 in table "two"
sql.deleteRow("two", 1); // rowId 1 is removed, but rowId 2 keeps its id
sql.selectCell("two", 2, 2); // returns "fifth"

## Constraints:

* `n == names.length == columns.length`
* `1 <= n <= 10^4`
* `1 <= names[i].length, row[i].length, name.length <= 10`
* `names[i]`, `row[i]`, and `name` consist of lowercase English letters.
* `1 <= columns[i] <= 10`
* All strings in `names` are unique.
* At most `2000` calls will be made to `insertRow`, `deleteRow`, and `selectCell` in total.

diagrams.caption: Deleting a row leaves its rowId empty; the next insert receives a new id

solutions.name: Sparse Row Map per Table
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store each table as a small object with a `nextRowId` counter and a hash map from row id to row values. Insert assigns the current counter, copies the row, and increments the counter. Delete removes exactly that row id. Select first finds the table, then looks up the row id and the 1-indexed column.

## Key Insight

The row id is part of the logical address. A deletion must remove the row without shifting any other row, so a sparse map matches the contract directly.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) average for insert, delete, and select.
- Space Complexity: O(total stored cells).

solutions.name: Tombstone Row Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep rows in insertion order inside each table. Because row ids start at 1 and grow by one, `rowId - 1` is the physical slot. Deleting a row writes a tombstone (`null`) into that slot instead of removing it. Future inserts append to the end, so they receive new row ids.

## Key Insight

An array is valid only if deleted slots remain as holes. Removing an element would renumber later rows and break every stored row id after the deletion point.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) for insert, delete, and select.
- Space Complexity: O(total cells ever inserted), including tombstoned row slots.

solutions.name: Flattened Cell Map
solutions.timeComplexity: O(c) insert, O(c) delete, O(1) average select
solutions.description:
## Approach

Flatten each cell into one hash-map key made from table name, row id, and column id. A second map stores the next row id per table, and another stores each table's column count. Insert writes one entry per column. Delete removes every cell key for that row. Select reads one flattened key.

## Key Insight

The cell address `(table, rowId, columnId)` is already unique. Flattening that address avoids storing row objects and makes select a single map lookup.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(c) for insert and delete for a table with c columns, O(1) average for select.
- Space Complexity: O(total stored cells).

solutions.name: Nested Row Array Maps
solutions.timeComplexity: O(c) insert, O(1) average delete and select
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use one outer hash map from table name to an inner hash map. The inner map stores `rowId -> String[]`, so selecting a cell avoids list overhead after insertion. A separate `nextRowId` map tracks the next id for each table. Delete removes one entry from the inner map.

## Key Insight

This is still sparse by row id, but the stored row is a compact array. It is useful when rows are immutable after insertion and reads dominate.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(c) to copy a row on insert, O(1) average for delete and select.
- Space Complexity: O(total stored cells).

solutions.name: Column-Oriented Tables
solutions.timeComplexity: O(c) insert, O(c) delete, O(1) average select
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent each table as a list of column maps. Column `j` maps row id to the value stored in that column. Insert writes the new row id into every column map. Delete removes the row id from every column map. Select chooses the requested column map and reads that row id.

## Key Insight

A column-store layout is a genuinely different model from row storage. It is especially natural when single-cell reads specify the column first and each column can be addressed independently.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(c) for insert and delete for c columns, O(1) average for select.
- Space Complexity: O(total stored cells).
